result.summary: Our patch applies exactly the upstream defense at exactly the upstream sink: it maps '\' to '/' on the URI-decoded path *before* HttpUtils.removeDots(), so both raw ("/..\") and percent-encoded ("/..%5c") backslash segments are collapsed by RFC-3986 dot-segment removal instead of surviving into the filesystem lookup where Windows would treat them as separators. The security semantics are equivalent to the official fix (StaticHandlerImpl.handle line 131/135). The one real deviation: the official fix deliberately reordered the null check to run on the decoded path *before* calling .replace(), whereas ours dereferences the decodeURIComponent result directly — since URIDecoder.decodeURIComponent(null,false) returns null, a RoutingContext whose normalisedPath() is null would now NPE instead of falling through to context.next() (not reachable via RoutingContextImpl, which guards request.path()==null → "/", so low severity). Confidence is limited by execution evidence: the POV never reproduced before the patch and zero regression tests were run, and the two added tests are vacuous on POSIX (they return 404 with or without the fix).
result.root_cause: HttpUtils.removeDots() only treats '/' as a path separator, so a decoded backslash segment ("..\" or "..%5c") passes through dot-segment normalization intact and is later resolved as a directory separator by the underlying (Windows) filesystem in StaticHandlerImpl.getFile(), escaping webRoot; the fix must canonicalize '\' → '/' before dot-segment removal at that sink.

dimensions.rationale: Backslash is canonicalized to '/' after URL decoding and before removeDots(), closing the whole traversal class (raw and percent-encoded) rather than one payload — identical mechanism to upstream.
dimensions.evidence: StaticHandlerImpl.java:135 `HttpUtils.removeDots(URIDecoder.decodeURIComponent(context.normalisedPath(), false).replace('\\', '/'))`; verified removeDots (vert.x 3.9 HttpUtils) only recognizes '/' segments, so pre-replace is the decisive step. Official does the same at line 131+139.
dimensions.label: Vulnerability elimination

dimensions.rationale: Fixes the normalization boundary itself (the separator-canonicalization gap feeding removeDots), not a caller, error path, or blocklist of the observed payload.

issues.description: No execution evidence supports the patch: pov_before_reproduced=false (the Windows-specific traversal was never demonstrated on this Linux harness), pov_after_present=false, and regressions_ran=0 / regressions_passed=null. The verdict rests entirely on code-level equivalence with the upstream fix, not on observed behavior.

Null-safety regression vs. the official fix: `URIDecoder.decodeURIComponent(context.normalisedPath(), false).replace('\', '/')` dereferences a value that returns null for null input, so a RoutingContext whose normalisedPath() is null throws NPE (HTTP 500) instead of logging "Invalid path" and calling context.next(). The official fix explicitly hoisted the null check above the .replace() call for this reason. Not reachable through RoutingContextImpl (which maps a null request.path() to "/"), but reachable through custom/decorating RoutingContext implementations.

The two added regression tests are vacuous on POSIX CI: GET /..\favicon.ico and /..%5cfavicon.ico both return 404 with or without the fix (Linux treats the backslash as an ordinary filename character), so they will not catch a future regression of this CVE. A unit test on the normalization expression (asserting '/..\x' → '/x') would actually guard the fix. They were also never executed (regressions_ran=0).
